title: Wayfinding for People With Dementia: A Review of the Role of Architectural Design
review_question: To provide an overview of the available literature on architectural wayfinding design for people with dementia in nursing homes, summarize the results, and substantiate them through an interdisciplinary interpretation, taking into account changes in the orientation process of people with dementia.
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Available literature on architectural wayfinding design for people with dementia in nursing homes was reviewed. The review focused on nursing homes because most empirical evidence is from those settings. Studies involving only people with Alzheimer's disease were noted, but caution was advised due to diagnostic limitations.

findings.antecedent: Straight circulation systems (floor plan typology)
findings.source: The most thought-provoking result of the data analysis concerning the architectural features of the floor plans is that the layout of the circulation system significantly affected the residents' orientation and was identified as the most influential environmental factor on a resident's wayfinding abilities. In straight circulation systems, residents were able to find their way better than in any layout that featured a shift in direction, such as L-shapes.

findings.antecedent: Floor plan designs vs. interventions (signage, furnishings, lighting, colors)
findings.consequent: Spatial orientation and wayfinding of people with dementia
findings.source: From the findings of the studies discussed here, it can be hypothesized that floor plan designs significantly support the spatial orientation and wayfinding of people with dementia. Although they play an important role in such people's orientation, interventions such as signage, furnishings, lighting, and colors cannot compensate for an adverse architectural design (Elmstahl et al., 1997; Marquardt & Schmieg, 2009; Passini et. al., 1998; 2000).
findings.quote: floor plan designs significantly support the spatial orientation and wayfinding... interventions... cannot compensate for an adverse architectural design

findings.antecedent: Simple, clear layout of the floor plan and well-defined, geometrically simple rooms (familiar design, not requiring new skills/strategies)
findings.consequent: Successful orientation and wayfinding in nursing homes
findings.source: A simple, clear layout of the floor plan and well-defined, geometrically simple rooms are structural prerequisites to successful orientation and wayfinding in nursing homes.
findings.quote: A simple, clear layout of the floor plan and well-defined, geometrically simple rooms are structural prerequisites to successful orientation and wayfinding

findings.antecedent: Visual access to all relevant places and ability to oversee entire immediate living environment
findings.consequent: Spatial orientation and wayfinding for people with dementia
findings.source: all places relevant to them should allow for visual access, and it should be possible for them to oversee their entire immediate living environment.
findings.quote: all places relevant to them should allow for visual access, and it should be possible for them to oversee their entire immediate living environment.

findings.antecedent: Avoidance of crossing hallways and several changes in direction; intuitive leading, not requiring choice from different options
findings.consequent: Wayfinding abilities for people with dementia
findings.source: crossing hallways and several changes in direction should be avoided. People should be led intuitively and not be required to choose from different options to plan a route.
findings.quote: crossing hallways and several changes in direction should be avoided. People should be led intuitively and not be required to choose from different options to plan a route.

findings.antecedent: Placing an eat-in kitchen or dining room at the point where direction changes in the circulation system
findings.source: If a floor plan typology that features changes in the direction of the circulation system is the only design option at a site, a meaningful reference point should be incorporated. Placing an eat-in kitchen or dining room at the point where direction changes in the circulation system constitutes an excel-lent reference point that can serve as a spatial anchor point for residents.
findings.quote: Placing an eat-in kitchen or dining room at the point where direction changes in the circulation system constitutes an excel-lent reference point

findings.antecedent: Distinctions in size, shape, color, and lighting for rooms with similar meaning/function
findings.consequent: Ability to identify and locate rooms
findings.source: Further, to identify and locate rooms with a similar meaning or function, distinctions in size, shape, color, and lighting must be articulated.
findings.quote: to identify and locate rooms with a similar meaning or function, distinctions in size, shape, color, and lighting must be articulated.

findings.antecedent: Function of rooms and other spaces made clearly legible by size, proportion, materials, and furnishings (creating distinctive places)
findings.source: The function of rooms and other spaces, as well as the behavior that is expected and appropriate there, can be made clearly legible by means of size, proportion, materials, and furnishings. In this manner, distinctive places that can better be memorized and located are created, thus promoting residents' spatial orientation and wayfinding.
findings.quote: The function of rooms and other spaces... can be made clearly legible by means of size, proportion, materials, and furnishings... promoting residents' spatial orientation and wayfinding.

synthesis_conclusions: Floor plan designs significantly support the spatial orientation and wayfinding of people with dementia.
Interventions such as signage, furnishings, lighting, and colors cannot compensate for an adverse architectural design.
For the creation of a supportive, dementia-friendly environment, both aspects of architectural design (floor plan typology and environmental cues) must be considered.

Design guidelines to support wayfinding abilities include: 1. No need for new or higher skills (simple, clear, familiar layouts). 2. Allow visual access and overview. 3. Reduce decision making. 4. Increase architectural legibility.
evidence_gaps: Additional research is needed to better understand the relationship between architectural design and human behavior.
The operational requirements of nursing homes in relation to floor plan typologies of facilities need to be investigated.
Further development of an evidence-based architecture for people with dementia is necessary.
limitations: The definitive diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease requires clinical syndrome and microscopic examination of the brain at autopsy, so studies enrolling only people with an AD diagnosis should be regarded with caution.

For studies comparing floor plan typologies (e.g., straight corridors), factors like length of corridors, lighting intensity, architectural differentiation, natural light, views to the outside, and other sensory stimulation were often not measured.
While the importance of good visual access was identified across studies, it was not always explicitly measured.

paper_metadata.crossref_title: Wayfinding for People with Dementia: A Review of the Role of Architectural Design
paper_metadata.crossref_journal: HERD: Health Environments Research & Design Journal
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Objective: This paper provides an overview of the available literature on architectural wayfinding design for people with dementia in nursing homes. The results were to be summarized and substantiated through an interdisciplinary interpretation, taking into account changes in the orientation process of people with dementia. Background: Spatial disorientation and declining wayfinding abilities are among the early symptoms of dementia, limiting a person's ability to perform activities of daily living (ADLs) independently and ultimately, perhaps leading to institutionalization. A prerequisite to maintaining residents' quality of life in a nursing home is their ability to orient themselves within their new environment. Approach: The available literature on wayfinding design for people with dementia in nursing homes was reviewed. Two aspects of interventions for residents' wayfinding abilities were identified: the design of the floor plan typology and environmental cues. Results: The design of the physical environment plays a major role in supporting the wayfinding abilities of people with dementia. The floor plan design of a nursing home in particular has a significant influence on residents' spatial orientation and wayfinding. Additional interventions such as signage, furnishing, lighting, and colors are additional supporting features but they cannot compensate for an adverse architectural design. Conclusions: For the creation of a supportive, dementia-friendly environment, both aspects of architectural design must be considered. Design guidelines to support the wayfinding abilities of people with dementia were developed to synthesize both.
